title: Advanced Linux Administration
subtitle: Jeopardy Review

jeopardyFormatExample.clueText: This command displays the first 10 lines of a file

categoryLegend: Files & Archives: head, cp -r, mkdir, touch, tar.  Permissions & ACLs: chown, sticky bit, minimum ACL, setfacl, getfacl.  Networking & DNS: ip link, ping -w, MX records, /etc/resolv.conf, Ctrl-C.  System & Shell: /etc/fstab, swap, uptime, let, shell comments.  Boot, Services & Legacy: Boot from Hard Disk, chkconfig, rcapache2, Traffic-vis, rsync.

clues.clue: This command displays the first 10 lines of a file by default, making it the quickest way to preview a log or config.
clues.explain: head reads only the start of a file (10 lines by default, or N with -n), so it returns instantly on huge logs instead of streaming the whole file like cat.

clues.clue: This cp flag causes the copy operation to descend into subdirectories, preserving the entire directory tree at the destination.
clues.explain: Without -r, cp refuses to copy a directory. The -r (recursive) flag walks every subdirectory, recreating the full tree at the destination.

clues.clue: This command creates a new, empty directory at the path you supply. Supply -p to also build any missing parent directories.
clues.explain: mkdir creates one directory; with -p it builds an entire missing path (a/b/c) in one call and won't error if parts already exist.

clues.clue: Running this command on an existing filename updates its access and modification timestamps to the current time; running it on a new filename creates an empty file.
clues.explain: touch's original job is updating a file's access/modify timestamps; as a side effect, naming a file that doesn't exist creates it empty -- the common way to make a placeholder.

clues.clue: This archive container format bundles multiple files and directories into a single file without compression by default; the .gz or .bz2 extension is added when a compressor is piped in.
clues.explain: tar bundles many files into one .tar archive but does not compress by default; piping through gzip or bzip2 (-z/-j) adds the .gz/.bz2 compression.

clues.clue: This command changes both the owning user and the owning group of a file in a single call, using the syntax user:group as its argument.
clues.explain: chown sets the owner; appending :group in one call also changes the group, saving a separate chgrp. chmod changes permission bits, not ownership.

clues.clue: Set on a shared directory such as /tmp, this special permission bit prevents users from deleting or renaming files that belong to other users.
clues.explain: On a world-writable dir like /tmp, the sticky bit (chmod +t) restricts deletion/rename to each file's owner (or root), so users can't remove each other's files.

clues.clue: Every file has this baseline ACL that mirrors the three standard Unix permission entries: owner, owning group, and other.
clues.response: What is the minimum ACL (owner, owning-group, other)?
clues.explain: A minimum ACL is just the classic three entries -- owner, group, other -- identical to standard rwx bits. Adding named users/groups makes it an extended ACL.

clues.clue: This command modifies a file's access control list, letting you grant or revoke permissions for named users or groups beyond the traditional owner/group/other model.
clues.explain: setfacl grants fine-grained per-user/per-group permissions beyond the single owner/group/other model -- e.g. give one extra user write access without changing the group.

clues.clue: This command reads and displays a file's full ACL in a human-readable format, showing every named user, named group, and mask entry.
clues.explain: getfacl displays the full ACL (named users, named groups, mask, defaults), letting you audit exactly who has what before changing it with setfacl.

clues.clue: This ip command variant brings a network interface named eth0 to an operational state, equivalent to the older ifconfig eth0 up.
clues.response: What is ip link set eth0 up?
clues.explain: This activates the interface so it can pass traffic; 'down' deactivates it. ip is the modern replacement for the deprecated ifconfig.

clues.clue: This ping flag sets a hard deadline in seconds; once the deadline expires the command exits regardless of how many packets have been sent.
clues.explain: -w sets a total deadline in seconds (ping stops when it elapses no matter what), versus -c which stops after a fixed packet count.

clues.clue: This DNS record type designates the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of a domain.
clues.response: What is an MX (Mail Exchanger) record?
clues.explain: An MX record names the host(s) that accept mail for a domain, with a priority; without it, senders can't find where to deliver email.

clues.clue: The Linux resolver reads this file to determine which DNS servers to query and what search domain to append to unqualified hostnames.
clues.explain: /etc/resolv.conf lists nameserver IPs and a search domain; the resolver consults it to turn hostnames into addresses (often managed by systemd-resolved/NetworkManager today).

clues.clue: While ping is running in a terminal, pressing this key combination sends SIGINT to the process, stopping it and printing the packet-loss summary.
clues.explain: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground process, which ping handles by stopping and printing its packet-loss/RTT summary. Ctrl-D sends EOF; Ctrl-Z suspends.

clues.clue: This system file contains the list of filesystems to mount at boot, including the swap partition and any additional block devices.
clues.explain: /etc/fstab lists filesystems and swap to mount at boot, each line giving the device, mount point, type, and options. A bad entry here can stop a boot.

clues.clue: This partition type acts as overflow RAM: the kernel pages out inactive memory segments to it so physical RAM can serve active processes.
clues.explain: Swap is disk space the kernel uses as overflow for RAM, paging out inactive memory so active processes keep physical RAM. It's slower than RAM -- a safety valve, not a speed boost.

clues.clue: This command prints how long the system has been running and displays three load-average figures representing the past 1, 5, and 15 minutes.
clues.explain: uptime shows time since boot plus 1/5/15-minute load averages -- the average number of processes wanting CPU, a quick health gauge (compare to core count).

clues.clue: This Bash built-in command performs integer arithmetic directly in a shell script, for example: let result=count+1.
clues.explain: let evaluates integer arithmetic in Bash (let x=2+3); alternatives are $(( )) and expr. It handles math that a plain assignment would treat as text.

clues.clue: In a shell script, every line that begins with this single character is treated as a comment and is ignored by the interpreter at runtime.
clues.explain: A # starts a comment to end of line (except in the #! shebang on line 1). The interpreter ignores it, so it documents code or disables lines.

clues.clue: On a SUSE installer boot menu, selecting this option bypasses the installation workflow and loads the operating system already present on the hard disk.
clues.response: What is "Boot from Hard Disk"? (SUSE installer boot-menu option)
clues.explain: On the SUSE install media's boot menu, this entry skips the installer and boots the OS already on disk -- what you pick to avoid reinstalling when the media is left in.

clues.clue: This legacy SysV command removes the apache2 web-server service from the init runlevels so it no longer starts automatically at boot. (Modern equivalent: systemctl disable apache2)
clues.response: What is chkconfig apache2 off? (modern: systemctl disable apache2)
clues.explain: chkconfig off removes the service from the SysV runlevels so it won't auto-start at boot (it doesn't stop a running copy). systemd replaced it with 'systemctl disable'.

clues.clue: On SUSE systems using SysV init, this rc-style wrapper script was the standard way to stop the apache2 service from the command line. (Modern equivalent: systemctl stop apache2)
clues.response: What is rcapache2 stop? (modern: systemctl stop apache2)
clues.explain: SUSE's rc<service> scripts wrap the SysV init script; 'rcapache2 stop' halts the running daemon now. systemd replaced it with 'systemctl stop apache2'.

clues.clue: This older network-analysis program visualizes active connections from the local host to remote hosts, showing which processes hold those connections. (Modern equivalent: iftop or ss)
clues.response: What is Traffic-vis? (modern: iftop or ss -tn)
clues.explain: Traffic-vis was an older tool that mapped active connections from the host to remote peers and the owning processes; iftop and ss -tn fill that role today.

clues.clue: This utility efficiently copies complete directory trees across a network to another computer, transferring only changed blocks and preserving permissions, making it the standard tool for remote backups.
clues.explain: rsync copies directory trees and, using its delta algorithm, transfers only changed blocks while preserving permissions -- making repeat backups and remote syncs fast.
